Keywords: Weep, And, The

outputs.L1:
Weep for the country in its present state,  
And for the gloom that still the future waits;  
The proud Confederate eagle heard the sound,  
And, in her flight, fell prostrate to the ground!

Weep for the loss the country has sustained,  
By which her now-dependent is in jail;  
For him who has survived the war, now grieve—  
For conscript husbands and the wives who weep!

Weep for the seas of blood the battle cost,  
And souls whose hope is ever, forever lost;  
For ravaged fields that no recruits restore,  
And trees by vengeance blasted to the core!

Weep for the downfall of your chiefs and heads,  
Who sank with no relief to stay their dread;  
Who fell beneath the hatchet of their pride,  
Then, like the serpent, bit themselves and died!

Weep for the downfall of your president,  
Who, far too late, his folly must repent;  
Who, like the dragon, did all heaven assail,  
And dragged his friends to limbo with his tail!

Weep o’er peculiar, swelling coffers void,  
Our treasures lost and all their banks destroyed;  
Their baseless notes, replete with shame for all,  
Each day awaiting their impending fall;  
In quest of profits never to be won,  
Now sadly fallen—forever lost and done!
outputs.L2:
Mourn the nation’s present plight  
And the darkness looming over its future.  
The haughty Confederate eagle heard the cry,  
Then plunged from the sky and lay defeated on the earth.

Lament the losses the country has endured,  
Through which one now dependent sits imprisoned;  
Grieve for the man who survived the war,  
For husbands taken by conscription and wives left in tears.

Sorrow over the oceans of blood spilled in battle  
And the souls whose hope has vanished forever;  
Mourn the devastated fields, with no one to restore them,  
And trees destroyed to their very roots by vengeance.

Grieve for the ruin that overtook your leaders and commander,  
Who went down with no means of rescue;  
Struck by the weapon of their own arrogance,  
They turned upon themselves like a serpent and died.

Mourn the collapse of your president,  
Who recognized his foolishness only when it was too late;  
Like a dragon, he challenged all of heaven  
And swept his companions into limbo behind him.

Lament the strangely swollen coffers now emptied,  
The vanished wealth and the destruction of every bank;  
Their worthless notes have brought disgrace upon everyone,  
While each day they await their ultimate failure.  
They pursued gains that could never be secured,  
Only to fall in sorrow and remain ruined forever.
outputs.L3:
The poem mourns the devastation of the country and the bleak future that follows the collapse of the Confederacy. It portrays a society overwhelmed by defeat, instability, and despair, with little hope of recovering what has been lost. Particular attention is given to the suffering endured by soldiers and their families: imprisonment, forced conscription, bereavement, and prolonged hardship have left deep emotional and physical wounds.

The speaker also grieves over the war’s immense human cost. Countless lives have been lost, blood has been shed on a vast scale, and homes and communities have been destroyed. At the same time, the poem condemns Confederate leaders, including the president, whose pride, poor judgment, and reckless ambitions are presented as major causes of the catastrophe. In pursuing their goals, they have brought ruin not only upon themselves but also upon those who trusted and supported them.

Finally, the poem deplores the collapse of the financial system in the aftermath of the war. Treasuries have been emptied, banks destroyed, and currency rendered worthless. This economic devastation intensifies the broader sense of loss, showing that the Confederacy’s defeat has shattered political authority, social stability, and material security alike.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a sustained lament for the defeated Confederacy, using the repeated command to “weep” as both a refrain and a judgment. Each repetition introduces another dimension of the catastrophe left by the Civil War. The speaker first evokes the battlefield, where bloodshed and death have destroyed armies and ended hopes of victory. The focus then widens to the surviving soldiers, many of whom are wounded, imprisoned, or returning home to lives permanently altered by war. Their suffering is joined by that of grieving parents, widows, children, and other family members who must endure the absence or death of loved ones.

The devastation extends beyond individual loss. The poem portrays the South as a ruined landscape marked by damaged homes, wasted fields, and shattered communities. Political leaders and military commanders have failed, while the institutions that supported the Confederate project have collapsed. Financial destruction completes the picture: property, currency, investments, and expectations of prosperity have become worthless. In this way, military defeat is shown to have produced social, political, and economic disintegration.

Although the poem mourns these losses, it does not treat them as merely accidental or undeserved. Its conclusion identifies pride, folly, and rebellion as the causes of the disaster. The Confederacy’s downfall is therefore presented as the consequence of its own choices rather than simply the result of superior enemy power. The repeated calls to mourn gradually become an indictment of the ambitions that led to war.

By bringing together battlefield slaughter, imprisonment, private grief, environmental ruin, failed leadership, and financial collapse, the poem depicts Confederate defeat as total. Its elegiac language expresses sorrow for those who suffered, but its moral emphasis remains clear: the Confederate cause produced devastation for its supporters and brought ruin upon the society that pursued it.
outputs.L5:
### Weep, And The World Softens

Weep, and let the sorrow leave you. Tears are not signs of weakness; they are the quiet language of a heart carrying too much.

The world may not stop when you cry. Morning will still arrive, streets will fill, and clocks will continue their patient turning. Yet something within you may soften. What once felt unbearable may become lighter, not because it has vanished, but because you no longer hold it in silence.

Weep for what was lost. Weep for what never came to be. And when the tears finally slow, breathe deeply.

The world is still here—and so are you.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 19th-century-style lament poem mourning the defeat of the Confederacy, the devastation of war, the imprisonment of its leaders, and the collapse of its currency and banks.
counterfactuals.output:
**Lament for a Fallen South**

The bugle sleeps upon the field,  
The drum is hushed and torn;  
No more beneath the starry fold  
The weary ranks are borne.  
By wasted farm and blackened mill,  
Where spectral chimneys stand,  
The widow hears the winter wind  
Go mourning through the land.

The sabres rust, the banners fade,  
The cannon sink in clay;  
The sons who marched with songs at dawn  
Lie nameless far away.  
From Shenandoah’s ruined vale  
To Georgia’s trampled loam,  
The crow alone keeps sentinel  
Above the roofless home.

In guarded cell the chieftains wait,  
Their seals and swords denied;  
The doors of council echo bare,  
Their ancient boastings died.  
No courier rides the midnight road,  
No gray-clad guard replies—  
A conquered dream, in irons bound,  
Beneath estranging skies.

The Treasury’s proud paper notes  
Are leaves the merchants scorn;  
The banker bars his empty vault  
And greets a beggared morn.  
The ledgers tell of vanished gold,  
Of credit turned to dust;  
The planter’s bond, the soldier’s pay,  
Are ashes in his trust.

Yet deeper than the cities burned,  
Or wealth swept out to sea,  
There haunts the cause a darker grief—  
The chains of slavery.  
No honest hymn may mourn the fall  
And veil that captive cry;  
The old world perished by the wrong  
It labored to deny.

So toll, sad bell, for all who fell,  
For blue and gray alike;  
For mothers bent beside the hearth,  
For homes the armies strike.  
But let no sorrow crown the chain  
Nor bid its shadow rise:  
From ruin may a juster land  
Stand chastened ’neath the skies.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a satirical elegy about the Confederacy’s downfall, using repeated lines beginning with “Weep,” biblical imagery, and references to Jefferson Davis, conscription, battlefield deaths, and financial ruin.
counterfactuals.output:
**Lamentation for a Lost Cause**

Weep, daughters of Dixie, in bombazine gloom,  
For the kingdom of cotton has entered the tomb;  
Its Pharaohs lie speechless, their ledgers unblessed,  
And the moth takes the gray coat, the grave takes the rest.

Weep, Jefferson Davis, beneath your thorn crown—  
No Gabriel comes riding to rescue the town;  
Your promised new Zion, so gallant in breath,  
Paid wages in paper and dividends in death.

Weep, conscripted plowboy, torn from the field,  
With a musket for manna, starvation for shield;  
The rich kept their silver, the poor kept the line,  
While generals read Joshua and squandered the wine.

Weep, Shiloh and Gettysburg, Wilderness red,  
Where trumpet and scripture made harvests of dead;  
The widow received, by executive grace,  
A flag, a condolence, and hunger’s embrace.

Weep, treasury notes, once proclaimed good as gold,  
Now fit to wrap herrings or kindle the cold;  
The banks have found Babylon, merchants despair—  
A fortune buys breakfast, if breakfast is there.

Weep, proud little empire of auction and chain,  
Your cornerstone crumbled beneath its own stain;  
No ark bore your covenant over the foam—  
The whirlwind was mustered, and judgment came home.

Weep, but weep wisely: let mourning confess  
That pomp cannot sanctify bondage’s dress;  
The Lost Cause is lost—let the plain record say:  
It marched under banners and squandered away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an archaic Civil War poem from the perspective of a Southern observer reflecting bitterly on the Confederacy’s collapse and its president’s folly.
counterfactuals.output:
**Lamentation Beneath the Fallen Stars**

The drums are dumb on Richmond’s hill,  
The cannon’s wrath is done;  
Our tattered stars, at morning chill,  
Hang shamefaced from the sun.  
The James flows black by ashen quays,  
Where pride went forth in flame;  
And widows count the empty days  
That bear no victor’s name.  

O Davis, throned in counsel’s mist,  
What phantoms ruled thy sight?  
Thou mad’st a kingdom of the fist  
And called its bondage right.  
Whilst hunger gnawed the soldier’s wife,  
And barefoot legions bled,  
Thy ministers still diced with life,  
And feasted with the dead.  

We boasted Rome in every street,  
Yet built on shackled breath;  
We sang of honor, brave and sweet,  
And sowed a field of death.  
The trumpet’s lie, the planter’s gold,  
The preacher’s wrathful plea—  
All could not make the wrong grow old,  
Nor sanctify the free.  

Now Lee hath yielded up the sword,  
The gray ranks melt away;  
No angel guards our ruined lord,  
No dawn redeems the day.  
The courthouse road is thick with men  
Who stare, yet dare not weep;  
They shall not see their homes again  
As those they swore to keep.  

I loved this land—its pines, its rain,  
Its red and wounded clay;  
Yet love must speak the bitter stain  
That banners hid away.  
For statesmen’s pride and masters’ claim  
Our fairest youth were slain;  
And he who staked a world on shame  
Hath harvested but pain.  

So fold the flag; let silence fall  
Where vaunting voices rang.  
No marble arch, no laurel wall,  
Can cleanse the chain’s iron clang.  
The South lies low—not fate alone,  
Nor Northern steel the cause:  
We raised our doom upon a throne  
Of folly, blood, and laws.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a rhyming historical poem in the style of a post–American Civil War broadside. Include a fallen eagle, weeping wives, seas of blood, ruined fields, defeated leaders, empty coffers, and worthless banknotes.
counterfactuals.output:
## **THE NATION’S LAMENT**  
*Printed for the People, in the Year of Peace*

Come gather near, both rich and poor, and hear the solemn tale,  
Of cannon smoke and shattered oak, of widow’s midnight wail;  
The fallen eagle stained the dust, his pinions torn and red,  
While Freedom bowed her laurel crown above the countless dead.  

The weeping wives at cottage doors looked down the lonesome lane,  
But those who marched with drums at dawn came never home again;  
Their candles waned, their children cried, the church bells tolled full slow,  
And every hearth kept one cold chair for him laid long ago.  

Through seas of blood the armies passed beneath a brazen sky,  
Where brother faced his brother’s gun and watched his comrade die;  
The rivers bore the battle’s stain, the wells were choked with clay,  
And Death, upon his ashen horse, rode proudly through the fray.  

The ruined fields grew thorns instead of cotton, corn, or rye,  
The barns stood black, the fences fell, no lark was heard on high;  
The plow lay rusting in the weeds, the mill wheel ceased to turn,  
And hungry hands raked barren earth where harvest fires had burned.  

Defeated leaders, pale and worn, put sword and seal away,  
Their banners furled, their councils hushed, their armies turned to clay;  
No trumpet now proclaimed their names, no cheering shook the street—  
They learned how brief is earthly pride, how bitter is defeat.  

The coffers yawned as empty vaults, the public gold was gone,  
While creditors with ledgers grim came knocking before dawn;  
Worthless banknotes filled the tills, though fortunes once they seemed—  
Now children folded paper boats from wealth their fathers dreamed.  

O North, O South, count well the cost that wrath and glory bring:  
No victor’s wreath restores the dead, no anthem cures war’s sting;  
Let justice mend the broken chain, let mercy sow the plain,  
That peace may raise a kinder crop where hatred planted pain.  

Then lift the eagle from the dust and bind his wounded wing;  
Let hammers sound where muskets roared, let schoolhouse voices sing;  
And where the wives once wept alone beneath the cypress tree,  
May Union walk with humbled heart, and all the land be free.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a long, somber poem titled “Weep for the Country,” portraying the human, political, military, and economic consequences of the Confederate defeat.
counterfactuals.output:
# Weep for the Country

Weep for the country, but not for the chain  
Struck from the captive’s wrist in righteous thunder;  
Not for the auction block, the whip, the stain,  
The families sold and torn from one another.  
Weep that so many years of pride and wrong  
Required the cannon’s mouth to answer stronger;  
That justice, waited for and thwarted long,  
Came clothed in fire because it could wait no longer.

Weep for the country, field by ruined field,  
Where wheat once whispered, corn stood green and tall;  
Where iron harvests made the valleys yield  
A crop of crosses by a churchyard wall.  
The fences vanished into bivouac flame,  
The orchard limbs were splintered by the shell;  
And every quiet creek acquired a name  
That widows afterward remembered well.

Weep for the country, where the marching feet  
Beat dust from roads beneath a pitiless sun;  
Where barefoot boys, half-starved, pursued retreat,  
Too young to know what pride had made them run.  
Gray coats grew brown with weather, blood, and clay;  
The drums fell silent, one by one, at last.  
A flag was folded on a sullen day,  
And armies entered memory and the past.

At Appomattox, hunger stacked its guns.  
No trumpet could persuade the dead to rise.  
The old cause ended with exhausted sons  
Who saw no victory in their comrades’ eyes.  
Some turned toward farms whose barns were only smoke,  
Toward roofless rooms and chimneys standing lone;  
Some bore a cough, a shattered hand, a yoke  
Of dreams that would not leave their sleep alone.

Weep for the mothers listening at the gate,  
Although no hoofbeat sounded down the lane;  
For wives who learned from lists or letters late  
That hope had been outlived by grief and rain.  
For children asking why the chair stayed bare,  
Why Father’s coat remained upon the wall;  
For sisters cutting mourning from despair,  
And bells that tolled until they tired of all.

Weep for the wounded laid on boards and straw,  
For surgeons working red from dusk to dawn;  
For fever, hunger, gangrene, tooth and saw,  
For nameless graves before the troops moved on.  
The blue and gray lay mingled in the mud,  
No argument remaining in the breath;  
The earth accepted every kind of blood,  
And uniforms were equalized by death.

Weep for the prisoners behind the wire,  
For rationed crusts, for winter’s naked cold;  
For eyes that watched the burial trenches tire,  
For bodies failing long before they grew old.  
No anthem warmed the bunks where sickness spread,  
No speech restored the wasted flesh and bone;  
The living counted footsteps of the dead  
And wondered whether home still meant a home.

Weep for the cities entered under flame,  
For Richmond’s warehouses against the sky;  
For streets that bore the ashes of a name,  
While sparks went wheeling upward, wild and high.  
The ledgers curled, the bridges groaned and fell,  
The foundries cooled, the shops were shuttered fast;  
And smoke became a dark, funereal veil  
Drawn over what had thought itself would last.

Weep for the currency made worthless scraps,  
For promises that could not purchase bread;  
For empty banks and half-erased old maps,  
For commerce stalled and credit lying dead.  
The railways twisted, depots burned away,  
The river trade stood broken at the pier;  
A month’s hard labor bought less every day,  
And famine followed closely after fear.

The planter saw his measured acres remain,  
Yet found the world that fed them overturned;  
The poor white farmer shouldered debt and pain,  
And sowed in soil the marching armies burned.  
The merchant swept the glass from off his floor;  
The blacksmith waited, lacking coal and steel;  
The veteran begged beside the courthouse door,  
His empty sleeve a wound no law could heal.

But weep not for the legal right to own  
A breathing soul beneath a bill of sale;  
That kingdom merited its broken throne,  
That commerce merited its ending wail.  
Four million people faced the uncertain morn,  
No longer property, though scarcely free—  
Released from bondage, into hunger born,  
With liberty proclaimed, but no guarantee.

Weep for the freedmen searching road and town  
For children taken years before the war;  
For mothers asking, writing names down,  
And walking miles to knock at one door more.  
For marriages at last acknowledged true,  
For schools in cabins, letters slowly learned;  
For wages stolen when the season grew,  
And justice promised, postponed, or overturned.

The ballots briefly opened like a spring;  
New voices rose in legislating halls.  
Yet terror answered every hopeful thing  
With midnight riders, torches, masks, and calls.  
The old dominion, beaten in the field,  
Sought other weapons, subtler than the sword:  
A labor trapped, a polling place concealed,  
A courtroom where the lie became the word.

Weep for a peace unfinished and unkept,  
For amendments grandly written, weakly guarded;  
For federal graves where Reconstruction slept,  
For citizens betrayed and hopes discarded.  
The slave was free—and freedom was no lie—  
Yet freedom starved when law refused its bread;  
A nation praised equality on high  
While segregation gathered strength instead.

Weep for the politics of bayonet and oath,  
For governments suspected, bought, or brave;  
For Southern anger hardening into growth,  
For Northern weariness that ceased to save.  
Some came to build, some came to steal and boast;  
Some local leaders served, and some deceived.  
Between the courthouse and the army post,  
A wounded public trusted—or believed.

Weep for the bitterness that memory made,  
When loss was polished into noble myth;  
When slavery’s cause was hidden in the shade  
And gallant suffering took the place of truth.  
The dead were used to sanctify the wrong;  
Defeat was dressed in moonlight, soft and pure.  
A nation taught its children half a song,  
Then wondered why its hatreds could endure.

For sorrow is not innocence, nor pain  
A proof that every banner carried justice.  
The conquered heart may honestly complain,  
Yet grief cannot make bondage fair or righteous.  
Still, grief is grief: the soldier’s mother weeps  
Though politicians lied about the fight;  
And every grave its human silence keeps,  
Beyond the reach of victory or right.

Weep for the country, North and South alike,  
For draft-riot streets and farms deprived of sons;  
For factories feeding powder to the strike,  
For fortunes multiplied by making guns.  
For taxes, pensions, debts no peace could end,  
For amputees beside the turning wheel;  
For households forced to borrow, sell, and spend,  
And decades needed for the land to heal.

Weep for the horses fallen in the trace,  
For mills dismantled, livestock driven away;  
For hunger written on a child’s thin face,  
For women planting fields from break of day.  
For counties where the taxable wealth was gone,  
Where roads dissolved and schoolhouse windows broke;  
Where every difficult, diminished dawn  
Rose through the taste of cinders and of smoke.

Weep for the veterans who could not explain  
Why sudden noises drew them back to slaughter;  
Who drowned their recollections deep in grain,  
Or named the dead to every son and daughter.  
Some spoke forever; others never spoke.  
Some kept a bullet near the heart or spine.  
Some wore old valor like a winter cloak;  
Some cursed the generals and the grand design.

Weep for the nation, reunited—how?  
By signatures that could not reconcile;  
By loyalty demanded in the now,  
While graves ran on for mile and mourning mile.  
The Union lived, but union is not breath  
Restored at once when fever leaves the frame;  
A state may rise politically from death  
And still be haunted by its former name.

The Capitol stood; the Constitution grew;  
The rebel governments and armies ceased.  
A broader promise struggled into view,  
Yet law alone could not establish peace.  
For peace is more than muskets put aside,  
More than surrender written, sealed, and read;  
It asks that truth and mercy both abide  
Among the living and beside the dead.

So weep for the country—not because  
A slaveholding rebellion lost its claim;  
Weep for the cost of cleansing broken laws,  
For all consumed within the cleansing flame.  
Weep that emancipation’s trumpet call  
Was purchased by such multitudes of graves;  
That those who built the wealth and bore it all  
Received so little when no longer slaves.

Weep for each soldier under marble stone,  
But do not carve the cause away with sorrow.  
Weep for each widow facing night alone,  
But tell the whole truth to the child tomorrow.  
Say courage served both mercy and mistake;  
Say honor cannot make injustice just.  
Say nations, like the human heart, may break  
When power is worshiped and the weak are crushed.

And when magnolias open after rain,  
When cotton fields lie silvered under morning,  
Remember beauty does not cancel pain,  
Nor pageantry relieve the past of warning.  
Beneath the courthouse statue’s weathered gaze,  
Beneath the pines where old encampments stood,  
Let honest memory walk the shadowed ways  
And name both human valor and human blood.

Weep for the country, chastened, changed, and scarred,  
Whose victory left duties yet undone;  
Whose freedom, born through years unspeakably hard,  
Was not completed when the war was won.  
Weep—and then labor, lest the ancient chain  
Be forged anew in custom, fear, or creed;  
Lest flags and myths make suffering vain,  
And pride again be watered into seed.

Weep for the country, but with open eyes.  
Let no soft legend quiet what was spoken:  
A house divided paid a dreadful price;  
A cruel foundation left the nation broken.  
The guns are still, yet history’s echoes roll—  
Through wealth and want, through ballot, school, and grave.  
Weep for the country; then repair its soul,  
And make the freedom won a freedom brave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
